goals: Explain how the drain of wealth, the ruin of crafts and peasant distress fed nationalism

Explain how the Press spread political awareness

slides.heading: Why did Indians begin to feel like one nation?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **economic exploitation**, **repressive policies** and the **Press**.

nodes.label: Ruin of crafts and peasant distress

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the drain of wealth, the ruin of crafts and peasant distress, Lord Lytton's measures, the Ilbert Bill controversy and the role of the Press
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: In the second half of the nineteenth century, people in Bengal, Bombay, Madras and Punjab began to think of themselves as Indians with common interests. Why? In this part we look at three streams: economic hardship under colonial rule, laws that treated Indians unequally, and newspapers that carried these grievances to readers across the country.

slides.heading: Four streams, one feeling
slides.body_md: Exploitation, repression, reform and the Press all fed **national feeling**.

visual.caption: Four streams that fed one national feeling.

slides.narration: This hub diagram shows four streams that flowed into Indian nationalism. Economic exploitation and repressive policies created grievances. Reform movements gave Indians self-respect and unity. The Press carried ideas to readers everywhere. In this part we study exploitation, repression and the Press; reform comes in Part 2.

slides.heading: The drain of wealth
slides.body_md: Wealth flowed to **Britain** without an equal return, as **Dadabhai Naoroji** argued.

nodes.label: Salaries and pensions of British officials
Home charges and interest on loans
Wealth reaches Britain without equal return

visual.alt: Flow of the drain of wealth: Indian revenues and trade pay for salaries and pensions of British officials, home charges and interest on loans, and profits of British firms, so wealth reaches Britain without an equal return
visual.caption: The drain, as the early nationalists described it.

slides.narration: Early nationalists, led by Dadabhai Naoroji, argued that India's wealth was being drained to Britain. Salaries and pensions of British officials, charges paid in London, interest on loans and the profits of British firms all left the country. Nothing equal came back. This argument turned poverty from a matter of fate into a criticism of colonial rule.

slides.heading: Ruin of handicrafts
slides.body_md: Cheap **machine-made** goods and one-sided duties destroyed **artisan** livelihoods.

rows: Cheap machine-made British cloth enters India
Local weavers cannot match the price
Indian goods face high duties in Britain
Courts and nobles who bought fine crafts decline
Home demand for luxury goods falls
Artisans move to farming as labourers
More pressure on land and more poverty

visual.alt: Table of changes and their effects on artisans: cheap British machine cloth undercuts weavers, Indian goods face high duties in Britain, old patrons decline, and artisans move to farm labour, adding pressure on land
visual.caption: Imagined classroom summary of a well-known trend.

slides.narration: India had been famous for fine cloth. In the nineteenth century, cheap machine-made cloth from British factories entered Indian markets, while Indian goods faced high duties in Britain. Old patrons such as royal courts declined. Many weavers and other artisans lost their work and became farm labourers. Nationalists pointed to this as proof that colonial rule served British interests.

slides.heading: Peasants and famines
slides.body_md: Heavy **land revenue**, **debt** and slow **famine relief**.

nodes.label: Payment due even in bad seasons
Loans from moneylenders at high interest
Famine relief seen as too little

visual.alt: Flow of peasant distress: heavy land revenue due even in bad seasons leads to loans at high interest, loss of land and poverty, and famine relief is seen as too little
visual.caption: Why villages grew restless.

slides.narration: Peasants paid a heavy land revenue, and it fell due even when the rains failed. To pay it, many borrowed from moneylenders at high interest and slowly lost their land. During the great famine of eighteen seventy-six to seventy-eight, relief was widely seen as too little and too late. Rural distress became one more grievance against the government.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: sorting grievances
slides.body_md: Is each imagined grievance **economic** or caused by a **repressive law**?
bullets: Step 1: does it concern **livelihood, money or land**? Economic.
Step 2: does a **law** treat Indians **unequally** or silence them? Repressive.
Step 3: name the law where you can.

rows: A weaver's looms stand idle because mill cloth is cheaper
A teacher must apply for a licence to keep a gun his European neighbour keeps freely
A Marathi weekly is warned for criticising famine relief
A farmer borrows to pay revenue after a failed monsoon

visual.alt: Worked example table sorting four imagined grievances: idle looms and a farmer borrowing for revenue are economic; a licence for a gun and a warned Marathi weekly are repressive measures
visual.caption: Ask: is the cause about money and livelihood, or about a law that treats Indians unequally?

slides.narration: Let us sort four imagined grievances. A weaver whose looms stand idle because mill cloth is cheaper has an economic grievance. A farmer who borrows to pay revenue after a failed monsoon also has an economic one. A teacher who needs a licence for a gun that his European neighbour keeps freely faces the Arms Act. A Marathi weekly warned for criticising famine relief faces the Press Act.

slides.heading: Lord Lytton's measures
slides.body_md: The **Durbar (1877)**, the **Vernacular Press Act (1878)** and the **Arms Act (1878)**.

rows: Delhi Durbar to proclaim the Queen Empress of India
Lavish spending during a severe famine
Curbed Indian-language papers; English papers left free
Licence needed by Indians; Europeans exempt

visual.alt: Table of Lord Lytton's measures: the Delhi Durbar of 1877 during a famine, the Vernacular Press Act of 1878 that curbed Indian-language papers only, and the Arms Act of 1878 that required Indians but not Europeans to hold licences

slides.narration: Lord Lytton was Viceroy from eighteen seventy-six to eighteen eighty. In eighteen seventy-seven he held a grand Durbar in Delhi to proclaim Queen Victoria Empress of India, while millions suffered in a famine. In eighteen seventy-eight came the Vernacular Press Act, which curbed newspapers in Indian languages, and the Arms Act, which required Indians but not Europeans to hold licences for arms.

slides.heading: Quick check: who introduced the Bill?
slides.body_md: True or false: the Ilbert Bill was introduced under Lord Ripon.
slides.narration: Lytton was followed by a different viceroy. Was the Ilbert Bill introduced in his time?

slides.heading: The Ilbert Bill controversy, 1883
slides.body_md: A Bill to let **Indian judges** try **Europeans** met fierce European protest.

nodes.label: 1883: Bill lets Indian judges try Europeans
Government gives way and dilutes the Bill
Indians learn the value of organised protest

visual.alt: Flow of the Ilbert Bill controversy: in 1883 a Bill to let Indian judges try Europeans meets loud European protest, the government dilutes it, and Indians see racial prejudice and learn the value of organised protest
visual.caption: Under Lord Ripon, 1883.

slides.narration: Under Lord Ripon, the Ilbert Bill of eighteen eighty-three proposed that qualified Indian judges could try Europeans in criminal cases. Many Europeans in India protested loudly, and the government gave way and diluted the Bill. Indians saw the racial prejudice behind the protest. They also learnt that organised, united agitation could change government policy, a lesson they soon applied themselves.

slides.heading: Why these measures mattered
columns:
**What Indians felt**

- Racial **inequality** in law
- Their **voice** being silenced
- **Indifference** to famine

**What Indians learnt**

- Grievances were **common** to all regions
- **Organised protest** could work
- An **all-India body** was needed

rows: Delhi Durbar to proclaim the Queen Empress of India
Lavish spending during a severe famine
Curbed Indian-language papers; English papers left free
Licence needed by Indians; Europeans exempt

visual.alt: Table of Lord Lytton's measures: the Delhi Durbar of 1877 during a famine, the Vernacular Press Act of 1878 that curbed Indian-language papers only, and the Arms Act of 1878 that required Indians but not Europeans to hold licences

slides.narration: Look at these measures in two ways. Indians felt that the law treated them as unequal, that their newspapers were being silenced and that their suffering in famine was ignored. They also learnt something. These grievances were shared across every region, and the Ilbert Bill showed that organised protest could succeed. Both feelings pointed towards a national organisation.

slides.heading: The nationalist Press
slides.body_md: Newspapers in **English** and **Indian languages** carried news and criticism far and wide.

visual.alt: Table of four nationalist newspapers: Amrita Bazar Patrika of Calcutta, Bengali and then English from 1878; The Hindu of Madras, founded in 1878; Kesari in Marathi linked with Tilak; and The Bengalee linked with Surendranath Banerjee

slides.narration: The second half of the nineteenth century saw a growth of nationalist newspapers. Amrita Bazar Patrika of Calcutta, The Hindu of Madras, Kesari in Marathi linked with Bal Gangadhar Tilak, and The Bengalee of Surendranath Banerjee are four examples. They reported government policies, criticised injustice and published the views of Indian leaders.

slides.heading: Quick check: why Indian languages?
slides.body_md: Why did newspapers in Indian languages matter so much?
slides.narration: Only a small number of Indians could read English. What did Indian-language papers add?

slides.heading: How the Press built opinion
slides.body_md: Report, **criticise**, carry ideas, **link regions**.

visual.alt: Flow of the Press's role: reporting events, criticising unjust measures, carrying leaders' ideas and linking readers across regions build a shared national opinion
visual.caption: How newspapers built opinion.

slides.narration: The Press worked in several ways at once. It reported events and policies. It criticised measures such as the Press Act and the Durbar. It carried the speeches and writings of leaders to people who never met them. Most important, a reader in Madras could learn about a grievance in Punjab, so people began to see their problems as shared.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a 10-mark answer in three parts
slides.body_md: Plan for: Press Act **[3]**, Arms Act **[3]**, Ilbert Bill and nationalism **[4]**.
bullets: Part (i): what the Act did **plus** why Indians objected: three clear points.
Part (ii): the rule, who was exempt, the effect on opinion.
Part (iii): the proposal, the protest, the outcome, and **two** lessons for nationalism.
Use the dates **1878** and **1883**, and name **Lytton** and **Ripon**.

slides.narration: Here is how to plan a ten-mark question on repressive measures. Give three clear points for the Press Act: what it did, whom it spared and why Indians objected. Do the same for the Arms Act. For the four-mark part on the Ilbert Bill, state the proposal, the European protest, the outcome, and two lessons Indians drew. Dates and the names of viceroys earn easy marks.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: **Drain of wealth** (Naoroji), **ruin of crafts**, **peasant debt** and **famine**.
**Lytton:** Durbar 1877, Vernacular Press Act 1878, Arms Act 1878.
**Ilbert Bill 1883** (Ripon): racial prejudice exposed; lesson of organised protest.
**Press:** Amrita Bazar Patrika, The Hindu, Kesari, The Bengalee spread awareness.

nodes.label: Lytton's Durbar, Press Act and Arms Act
Ilbert Bill: lesson of organised protest

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: the drain and ruin of crafts, peasant debt and famine, Lytton's Durbar, Press Act and Arms Act, the Ilbert Bill as a lesson in organised protest, and the Press spreading the message
visual.caption: Part 1 in five lines.

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. The drain of wealth, the ruin of crafts and peasant distress made Indians question colonial rule. Lord Lytton's Durbar, Press Act and Arms Act added a sense of humiliation. The Ilbert Bill exposed racial prejudice and showed the power of organised protest. And the Press carried all of this to readers across India.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Write **1878** for both the Press Act and the Arms Act; the Durbar was **1877**.
The Press Act hit **Indian-language** papers only; say so.
The Ilbert Bill: **1883**, **Ripon**, Indian judges trying **Europeans**.
For "factors of nationalism", link each factor to **how** it changed Indian feeling.
slides.narration: Some tips. Remember eighteen seventy-eight for both Acts and eighteen seventy-seven for the Durbar. Say clearly that the Press Act targeted Indian-language newspapers. For the Ilbert Bill, write eighteen eighty-three, Lord Ripon, and Indian judges trying Europeans. And when you list factors of nationalism, always explain how each one changed what Indians felt.

slides.heading: From reform to an all-India organisation
slides.body_md: Part 2 — four **reformers** and the founding of the **Indian National Congress**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: four reformers, Raja Rammohan Roy, Jyotiba Phule, Swami Dayananda Saraswati and Swami Vivekananda, and then the founding of the Indian National Congress
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Political grievances were only half the story. Reformers were also changing how Indians saw themselves. In this part we meet four of them, Raja Rammohan Roy, Jyotiba Phule, Swami Dayananda Saraswati and Swami Vivekananda, and then see how, in eighteen eighty-five, nationalists from all over India came together in the Indian National Congress.

slides.heading: Four reformers at a glance
slides.body_md: Each founded an organisation and attacked a different weakness of society.

rows: Against sati (banned 1829); modern education; women's rights
Education of girls and lower castes; against caste discrimination
Return to the Vedas; against caste by birth and child marriage
Chicago address 1893; service to the poor; self-confidence

slides.narration: Here are the four reformers. Raja Rammohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj in eighteen twenty-eight and fought against sati. Jyotiba Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj in eighteen seventy-three and worked for girls and the lower castes. Swami Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in eighteen seventy-five. Swami Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission in eighteen ninety-seven.

slides.narration: Raja Rammohan Roy, in Bengal, founded the Brahmo Samaj and campaigned until sati was declared illegal in eighteen twenty-nine. He also supported modern education and the rights of women. Jyotiba Phule, in Maharashtra, opened a school for girls in Pune with his wife Savitribai, and founded the Satyashodhak Samaj to fight discrimination against the lower castes.

questions.stem_md: Indian nationalists of the late nineteenth century used the phrase "drain of wealth". What did it describe?

options.text_md: The loss of water from canals in dry seasons
The transfer of India's wealth to Britain without an equal return to India
The movement of Indian traders to other Asian ports
The money spent by Indian princes on festivals

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The transfer of India's wealth to Britain without an equal return to India. The drain meant wealth leaving India for Britain (salaries and pensions of British officials, interest on loans, profits of British firms, home charges) with no matching return. The other options describe unrelated things.

questions.stem_md: Which early nationalist is best known for building the economic argument that British rule was draining India of its wealth?

options.text_md: Swami Vivekananda
Jyotiba Phule
A. O. Hume
Dadabhai Naoroji

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Dadabhai Naoroji. Dadabhai Naoroji set out the drain argument in his writings, including the book Poverty and Un-British Rule in India. Vivekananda and Phule were reformers; Hume was the founder of the Congress.

questions.stem_md: An imagined audit of 1882 lists two payments from Indian revenues. Payment P is a pension paid in London to a retired British official. Payment Q is the salary of an Indian clerk in Madras, who spends it in Madras shops. How would an early nationalist, using the drain argument, compare the two?

options.text_md: P is part of the drain because it leaves India without a return, while Q is not because the money stays in the Indian economy
Both are part of the drain, because both are paid out of Indian revenues
Neither is part of the drain, because both are lawful salaries or pensions
Only Q is part of the drain, because Indian clerks were paid less than British officials

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** P is part of the drain because it leaves India without a return, while Q is not because the money stays in the Indian economy. The drain argument looked at where the money went. A pension spent in Britain took wealth out of India with no return, while a clerk's salary spent in Madras circulated within India. Being paid from Indian revenue is not enough to make a payment part of the drain, being lawful is not the test, and the lower pay of Indians was a separate grievance.

questions.stem_md: An imagined district report of 1860 records that local handloom weavers' earnings have fallen steeply. The same report notes that raw cotton from the district sells well, the population is rising, and the bazaars are stocked with cheap cloth. Which explanation fits all of these details best?

options.text_md: High duties on Indian cloth in Britain closed the export market, and nothing else changed
The government banned the growing of cotton, so weavers ran short of thread
Cheap machine-made cloth from British factories undercut the weavers in their own bazaars, although cotton was plentiful and the population was growing
Demand for cloth fell sharply because the population shrank

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Cheap machine-made cloth from British factories undercut the weavers in their own bazaars, although cotton was plentiful and the population was growing. Only competition from cheap imported cloth fits all three details: cotton was available and people needed cloth, yet weavers sold less. The duties in Britain did hurt Indian exports, but they do not explain why weavers lost out in their own bazaars. A cotton ban or a shrinking population contradicts the report.

questions.stem_md: An imagined village record of 1877 states that the harvest failed, the revenue demand stayed the same, and by the end of the year half the farmers had borrowed from moneylenders and several had sold land. Which feature of the revenue system best explains why one bad harvest led to land sales and not just a lean year?

options.text_md: Moneylenders charged interest, and that alone caused the land sales
Land revenue was collected only from merchants, who then raised prices for farmers
A fixed demand had to be paid whatever the harvest, so farmers borrowed to meet it
The government had suspended all revenue in famine years, so farmers spent their savings freely

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A fixed demand had to be paid whatever the harvest, so farmers borrowed to meet it. The revenue was a fixed demand that did not shrink with the harvest, so a failed crop forced farmers to borrow, and debt then led to loss of land. Interest made the debt heavier but does not explain why the borrowing began. The other options contradict the record, which says the demand stayed the same.

questions.stem_md: An imagined pamphlet of 1879 claims that the Delhi Durbar of 1877 was a cause of the famine of 1876–78. Which reply is most accurate?

options.text_md: The famine had begun in 1876, before the Durbar, so the Durbar did not cause it; nationalists criticised the lavish spending during the famine as insensitive
The claim is correct, because the money spent on the Durbar left the government with no grain to distribute
The claim is wrong, because the Durbar was held after the famine had ended in 1878
The claim is partly correct, because the Durbar was held in 1875, just before the famine began

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The famine had begun in 1876, before the Durbar, so the Durbar did not cause it; nationalists criticised the lavish spending during the famine as insensitive. The famine of 1876–78 began before the Durbar of 1877 and went on after it, so the Durbar cannot be its cause. What Indians objected to was the display and spending during a famine, which they read as indifference. The other options put the Durbar at the wrong time or credit it with a cause it did not have.

questions.stem_md: The grand Delhi Durbar of 1877, held while a famine was raging, was organised under which Viceroy?

options.text_md: Lord Ripon
Lord Curzon
Lord Dalhousie
Lord Lytton

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Lord Lytton. Lord Lytton (Viceroy 1876–80) held the Durbar of 1877 to proclaim Queen Victoria Empress of India. Ripon came after him, Curzon later, and Dalhousie before 1857.

questions.stem_md: Which statement correctly describes the Vernacular Press Act of 1878?

options.text_md: It gave all newspapers in India complete freedom
It allowed the government to curb newspapers published in Indian languages, but not English ones
It applied only to English-language newspapers owned by Europeans
It created the first Indian newspaper

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It allowed the government to curb newspapers published in Indian languages, but not English ones. The Act let the government act against Indian-language (vernacular) newspapers that criticised it, while English-language papers were left out, which Indians saw as discrimination. It did not give freedom or target only European papers.

questions.stem_md: An imagined lawyer in 1879 says the Arms Act of 1878 was only a normal safety rule, since any government may control weapons. Which reply best explains why many Indians still resented it?

options.text_md: The licence rule fell on Indians while Europeans were exempt, so they objected to the unequal treatment rather than to regulation as such
The Act made it illegal for anyone in India, including the police, to own a gun
The Act applied only in the princely states, which had no say in the matter
The licence fee was fixed so high that no Indian could ever pay it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The licence rule fell on Indians while Europeans were exempt, so they objected to the unequal treatment rather than to regulation as such. The grievance was discrimination: Indians needed licences and Europeans did not. A rule that applied to everyone equally would have been a different matter. The Act did not ban all weapons and did not apply only to princely states, and a prohibitive fee is not what it is known for.

questions.stem_md: What did the Ilbert Bill of 1883 propose?

options.text_md: That Europeans could no longer live in India
That Indian judges in the districts could try Europeans in criminal cases
That all judges in India must be British
That newspapers must be licensed every year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** That Indian judges in the districts could try Europeans in criminal cases. Introduced under Lord Ripon, the Bill sought to remove a racial bar so that qualified Indian judges and magistrates could try European offenders. It did not expel Europeans or make all judges British, and it had nothing to do with newspapers.

questions.stem_md: Europeans in India organised a strong protest against the Ilbert Bill and the government gave way. Which lesson did educated Indians most likely draw from this?

options.text_md: The government always ignores public protest
Only armed rebellion could change any law
Organised, united agitation can force the government to change its policy
Indians and Europeans were treated equally in law

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Organised, united agitation can force the government to change its policy. The success of the European agitation showed Indians the power of organised protest and exposed racial inequality, encouraging them to form their own all-India organisation. It disproves the other three statements.

questions.stem_md: Under which Viceroy was the Vernacular Press Act repealed in 1882?

options.text_md: Lord Lytton
Lord Canning
Lord Minto
Lord Ripon

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Lord Ripon. Lord Ripon repealed the Act in 1882, 4 years after Lytton had passed it. Canning was Viceroy in 1858 and Minto in the 1900s.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** After 1878, some Indian-language newspapers began to appear in English instead.

**Reason (R):** The Vernacular Press Act applied only to newspapers in Indian languages.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: because the Act covered only Indian-language papers, a paper that switched to English fell outside it, which is why some did so.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Many Indians regarded the Arms Act of 1878 as unjust.

**Reason (R):** The Arms Act and the Vernacular Press Act were passed in the same year.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are true, but R does not explain A: the Act was resented because it required Indians but not Europeans to hold licences. Being passed in the same year as another Act is a coincidence of date, not a reason for the resentment.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Arms Act of 1878 applied equally to Indians and Europeans.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Indians needed a licence to keep arms, while Europeans were exempt; the inequality is why the Act was resented.

questions.stem_md: The Vernacular Press Act and the Arms Act were both passed in the year ___ under Lord Lytton.
questions.solution_md: Both Acts were passed in 1878.

questions.stem_md: Imagined firm A in 1880 sends its profits to shareholders in Britain. Imagined firm B, owned by Indian merchants, invests its profits in a new mill in India. Which firm's profits would an early nationalist count in the drain of wealth, and what does the contrast show about how the drain was judged?
questions.solution_md: Firm A, with the test of where the money goes.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Firm A**: its profits leave India without a return, so they form part of the **drain**.
The contrast shows that the drain was judged by **where the money ends up**, not by who earns it: profits reinvested in India stay in the Indian economy.

marking_scheme.step: Test of where the money ends up

questions.stem_md: A student says the decline of Indian handicrafts affected nationalism only because artisans lost income. Explain why this is incomplete, using the way nationalists read the cause of the decline.
questions.solution_md: Income loss is only part; the cause was read as policy favouring British interests.

answer.model_answer_md: Nationalists did not treat the decline as natural change. They pointed to **cheap British machine goods** and **high duties on Indian goods in Britain** as policy, and concluded that British rule served **British interests**. So the ruin of crafts became a **political** complaint and not just a private loss.

marking_scheme.step: Loss of income is only part of the point
Cause read as policy serving British interests

questions.stem_md: Name any two measures of Lord Lytton that Indians regarded as repressive or insensitive.
questions.solution_md: Any two of the three.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **Vernacular Press Act, 1878**, which curbed Indian-language newspapers.
2. The **Arms Act, 1878**, which required Indians but not Europeans to hold arms licences. (Also: the **Delhi Durbar of 1877** during a famine.)

questions.stem_md: Two imagined readers disagree about the Ilbert Bill of 1883. One says the dilution of the Bill after European protest taught Indians that protest was useless. The other says it taught the opposite. Which reading better fits the growth of nationalism? Give reasons.
questions.solution_md: The second reading, from the outcome of the European protest.

answer.model_answer_md: The **second reading** fits better. European protest was **organised and united**, and the government changed its plan, so Indians learnt that **organised agitation** could shift policy. The episode also exposed **racial prejudice**, which made educated Indians want their own **all-India body**.

marking_scheme.step: Reasons from the outcome of the protest

questions.stem_md: In an imagined district in 1878, weavers are idle, peasants are in debt after a failed harvest, and an Indian clerk notes that British officials' pensions are paid from Indian revenue in London. Which of these three grievances could most easily draw support from educated Indians in other provinces who neither wove cloth nor owned land? Give reasons for your choice, and say why one other grievance was less likely to spread beyond its region.
questions.solution_md: The drain, because of its national scale; local grievances needed a wider argument.

answer.model_answer_md: The **drain of wealth**: it concerned **India's revenues as a whole**, so an educated clerk in any province could see its effect and argue about it in newspapers. The **weavers'** loss and the **peasants'** debt were first felt in particular **localities and occupations**, so they needed a wider argument, such as the drain, to be seen as one national problem.

marking_scheme.step: Reason: national scale of the drain
Why a local grievance spread less easily

questions.stem_md: Which reformer founded the Brahmo Samaj (as the Brahmo Sabha) in 1828?

options.text_md: Swami Dayananda Saraswati
Jyotiba Phule
Swami Vivekananda
Raja Rammohan Roy

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Raja Rammohan Roy. Raja Rammohan Roy started the Brahmo Sabha, later the Brahmo Samaj, in Calcutta in 1828. Dayananda founded the Arya Samaj, Phule the Satyashodhak Samaj and Vivekananda the Ramakrishna Mission.

questions.stem_md: Raja Rammohan Roy's long campaign helped bring about a regulation of 1829 under Lord William Bentinck. What did it do?

options.text_md: It made English the only language of courts
It set up the first university in India
It declared the practice of sati illegal
It abolished the caste system by law

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It declared the practice of sati illegal. The 1829 regulation banned sati, the burning of widows, after Roy's campaign. The other options are not what the regulation did.

questions.stem_md: An imagined student claims that Raja Rammohan Roy's campaign against sati succeeded because the Indian National Congress pressed the government to act. Which reply is most accurate?

options.text_md: It is right: the Congress was founded to carry on Roy's campaign, so it was already pressing the government in 1829
It is wrong: the regulation of 1829 came 56 years before the Congress was founded in 1885, so Roy's campaign and the government under Lord William Bentinck explain it
It is wrong: the regulation of 1829 came after the founding of the Congress, but Roy had no part in it
It is right: Roy founded the Congress in 1828 with the aim of banning sati

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It is wrong: the regulation of 1829 came 56 years before the Congress was founded in 1885, so Roy's campaign and the government under Lord William Bentinck explain it. Sati was banned in 1829 and the Congress was founded in 1885, 56 years later, so it cannot have pressed for the ban. The ban followed Roy's long campaign and was issued under Lord William Bentinck. The other options misplace the Congress in time or credit Roy with founding it (he founded the Brahmo Samaj in 1828).

questions.stem_md: Jyotiba Phule founded which organisation in 1873 to work for the rights of the lower castes?

options.text_md: Satyashodhak Samaj
Arya Samaj
Prarthana Samaj
Ramakrishna Mission

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Satyashodhak Samaj. Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj (Society of Seekers of Truth) in 1873. The Arya Samaj was Dayananda's, the Prarthana Samaj a Bombay reform society, and the Ramakrishna Mission Vivekananda's.

questions.stem_md: An imagined student says: "Jyotiba Phule and Swami Dayananda Saraswati were doing the same thing, since both opposed caste distinctions." Which correction is most accurate?

options.text_md: They differed on caste: Phule defended caste by birth while Dayananda opposed it

Both opposed caste distinctions, but Phule's Satyashodhak Samaj worked for the rights and education of the lower castes and girls, whereas Dayananda's Arya Samaj sought reform through a return to the Vedas
They worked in the same organisation, the Arya Samaj, in different cities
Neither opposed caste distinctions; both worked only to spread English education

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both opposed caste distinctions, but Phule's Satyashodhak Samaj worked for the rights and education of the lower castes and girls, whereas Dayananda's Arya Samaj sought reform through a return to the Vedas. The student is right that both criticised caste, but the movements had different bases and aims: Phule's Satyashodhak Samaj (1873) centred on the rights and education of lower castes and girls, while Dayananda's Arya Samaj (1875) drew on the Vedas. They did not take opposite sides on caste, did not share an organisation, and neither worked only for English education.

questions.stem_md: In which year did Swami Dayananda Saraswati found the Arya Samaj?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 1875. The Arya Samaj was founded in 1875 (in Bombay). 1828 is the Brahmo Samaj, 1897 the Ramakrishna Mission and 1885 the Congress.

questions.stem_md: Swami Dayananda Saraswati urged Hindus to return to an earlier source of authority as a basis for reform. Which source was it?

options.text_md: The Vedas
The Mughal court chronicles
British law codes
Buddhist monastic rules

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Vedas. Dayananda regarded the Vedas as the true source of knowledge and called for a return to them, rejecting later practices such as idol worship and caste by birth. The other sources do not fit his teaching.

questions.stem_md: Swami Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission in which year?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 1897. The Ramakrishna Mission was founded in 1897. Vivekananda spoke at Chicago in 1893; 1875 is the Arya Samaj and 1906 the Muslim League.

questions.stem_md: An imagined student argues that Swami Vivekananda's address at Chicago in 1893 inspired the founders of the Indian National Congress to meet in 1885. Which reply is most accurate?

options.text_md: It did: the Chicago address of 1893 came first and led directly to the meeting at Bombay
It could not have: Vivekananda founded the Congress himself in 1897
It could not have: the Congress was founded in 1885, 8 years before the Chicago address, though the address may have strengthened Indian pride later
It did: the Ramakrishna Mission, founded in 1893, organised the first session

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It could not have: the Congress was founded in 1885, 8 years before the Chicago address, though the address may have strengthened Indian pride later. The Congress was founded in 1885 and the Chicago address came in 1893, 8 years later, so it cannot have inspired the first session. Its effect lay in the later growth of pride and self-confidence. The other options reverse the order of events or confuse the Mission (1897) with the Congress.

questions.stem_md: An imagined student says: "Reformers such as Phule and Dayananda talked about schools and caste, not about the government, so their work had nothing to do with the rise of nationalism." Which statement best qualifies this claim?

options.text_md: They did not campaign against British rule, but by building education, self-respect and unity they helped produce the confident public that later joined the national movement
The claim is wholly correct, because reformers opposed all political activity
The claim is wrong, because the reform movements were founded by the Indian National Congress
The claim is wrong, because the reformers demanded an immediate end to British rule

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** They did not campaign against British rule, but by building education, self-respect and unity they helped produce the confident public that later joined the national movement. The reformers worked mostly on society, so the student is right that they did not campaign against the government. But their work in education, self-respect and unity helped create people ready for national politics. The movements existed before the Congress and were not demands for ending British rule.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Vivekananda's address at Chicago in 1893 strengthened the self-confidence of educated Indians who had been taught to rate Western ideas above their own.

**Reason (R):** The address won respect for Indian thought from a Western audience.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: respect shown abroad to Indian thought answered the claim of Western superiority and encouraged Indians to value their own heritage.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Arya Samaj's call to return to the Vedas could be used to support reform rather than to resist it.

**Reason (R):** Dayananda used the Vedas to argue against caste by birth and child marriage.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: by arguing from the Vedas against caste by birth and child marriage, Dayananda turned a return to the old source into an argument for change.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Jyotiba Phule founded the Brahmo Samaj in Pune.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj (1873); the Brahmo Samaj was founded by Raja Rammohan Roy in Calcutta (1828).

questions.stem_md: Jyotiba Phule founded the ___ Samaj in 1873.
questions.solution_md: He founded the Satyashodhak Samaj.

questions.stem_md: Match each reformer with the organisation he founded.

options.text_md: Raja Rammohan Roy
Jyotiba Phule
Swami Dayananda Saraswati
Swami Vivekananda

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Roy: Brahmo Samaj; Phule: Satyashodhak Samaj; Dayananda: Arya Samaj; Vivekananda: Ramakrishna Mission.

questions.stem_md: Put the founding of four reform bodies and of the Indian National Congress into the order of their years.

options.text_md: Arya Samaj founded
Brahmo Samaj founded
Ramakrishna Mission founded
Indian National Congress founded
Satyashodhak Samaj founded

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: State two contributions of Raja Rammohan Roy to Indian society.
questions.solution_md: Any two contributions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. He campaigned against **sati**, which was banned in **1829**.
2. He founded the **Brahmo Samaj** (1828) and supported **modern education** and the rights of women.

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which Jyotiba Phule worked for the uplift of the oppressed.
questions.solution_md: Education and the Satyashodhak Samaj.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. With Savitribai Phule, he opened a **school for girls** in Pune and worked for the **education** of girls and lower castes.
2. He founded the **Satyashodhak Samaj (1873)** to fight **caste discrimination**.

questions.stem_md: An imagined student says: "Swami Dayananda Saraswati's call to return to the Vedas shows that he wanted to undo reform and keep society as it was." Use two features of the Arya Samaj's programme to assess this claim.
questions.solution_md: Misleading: the return to the Vedas was a basis for reform.

answer.model_answer_md: The claim is **misleading**. Dayananda used the **Vedas** as a basis for change: he opposed **caste by birth** and **child marriage** and backed **education**. Looking back to the Vedas also gave Indians **pride**, so the aim was renewal, not keeping society unchanged.

marking_scheme.step: Judgement that the claim is misleading, with reason

questions.stem_md: An imagined student says: "Swami Vivekananda awakened India only through his speech at Chicago in 1893." Use two facts to qualify this claim.
questions.solution_md: Partly right; qualified by the Mission and his teaching.

answer.model_answer_md: The Chicago address (**1893**) won respect abroad and made Indians **proud**, so the student is partly right. But he also founded the **Ramakrishna Mission (1897)** for **social service** and urged young Indians to be **fearless and self-reliant**, so his influence also worked through organisation and teaching at home.

marking_scheme.step: Chicago credited but not the whole story

questions.stem_md: Phule and Dayananda both opposed caste distinctions but built their movements on different bases. State the basis of each, and explain which movement was likelier to appeal to lower-caste groups who felt shut out of public life, giving a reason.
questions.solution_md: Phule: rights of lower castes; Dayananda: the Vedas; Phule likelier to appeal, with reason.

answer.model_answer_md: **Phule** built the Satyashodhak Samaj around the rights and education of the **lower castes** and girls; **Dayananda** built the Arya Samaj on a return to the **Vedas**. Phule's movement was likelier to appeal to excluded groups, since it was organised for them and challenged the **caste discrimination** they faced, while the Vedic appeal was framed around a shared ancient heritage.

questions.stem_md: The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 applied only to newspapers in Indian languages. Which inference about the government's thinking is best supported by this?

options.text_md: It believed English-language papers were never critical of its policies
It wished to protect Indian-language papers from unfair competition
It wished to end the printing of all newspapers in India
It believed Indian-language papers reached a wider public that could be roused against it, beyond the small English-educated group

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It believed Indian-language papers reached a wider public that could be roused against it, beyond the small English-educated group. Targeting only Indian-language papers suggests the government saw them as the ones that could stir ordinary readers, who could not read English. English papers could be critical too, so the second option overstates; the Act was not protective and did not end newspapers.

questions.stem_md: Kesari, a Marathi newspaper started in 1881, is most closely associated with which nationalist?

options.text_md: Surendranath Banerjee
Bal Gangadhar Tilak
W. C. Bonnerjee
Raja Rammohan Roy

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Bal Gangadhar Tilak. Kesari (Marathi) and Mahratta (English) were associated with Bal Gangadhar Tilak. Surendranath Banerjee ran The Bengalee.

questions.stem_md: The newspaper The Bengalee is associated with which leader?

options.text_md: Surendranath Banerjee
Dadabhai Naoroji
Jyotiba Phule
Lord Ripon

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Surendranath Banerjee. Surendranath Banerjee edited and ran The Bengalee. Naoroji, Phule and Ripon are not linked to it.

questions.stem_md: An imagined editor in 1879 argues: "My paper moved from Bengali to English and went on criticising the government, yet nothing happened to it. So the Vernacular Press Act cannot have been aimed at what we said." Which reading of the Act does this experience best support?

options.text_md: The Act punished only papers that praised the government
The Act's reach depended on the language of the paper and not on what it said, which is why Indians called it discriminatory
The Act applied only to English papers, so the editor had moved into its reach
The Act was repealed in 1878, so no paper was affected afterwards

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Act's reach depended on the language of the paper and not on what it said, which is why Indians called it discriminatory. A paper that kept the same criticism in English escaped the Act, which shows that the line was drawn by language. This is why Indians saw it as unfair to Indian-language papers. The Act did not target praise, covered Indian-language papers (not English), and was repealed only in 1882.

questions.stem_md: The Hindu, a nationalist English newspaper founded in 1878, was published from which city?

options.text_md: Calcutta
Lahore
Madras
Allahabad

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Madras. The Hindu was started in Madras in 1878. Calcutta, Lahore and Allahabad had other papers.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Newspapers in an Indian language usually carried news to readers in every province, whatever language those readers knew.

**Reason (R):** Readers of a paper in an Indian language were mostly people who knew that language.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false: a paper in one Indian language mostly reached readers of that language, so its reach was limited by language. R is true. Linking provinces needed other means, such as English-language papers and reports copied by editors elsewhere.

questions.stem_md: True or false? An English-language Indian newspaper in 1879 was outside the scope of the Vernacular Press Act.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** True. The Act covered newspapers in Indian languages, not those in English.

questions.stem_md: An imagined editor in 1880 prints in one issue a report on a revenue dispute in one province and a letter about the Arms Act from another. Explain one way this practice served nationalism that a local meeting could not, and one risk it carried for the editor under the law of the time.
questions.solution_md: Shared problems across provinces; risk under the Vernacular Press Act.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It put local grievances before readers in **many provinces**, so they began to see **shared problems**; a local meeting reached only those present.
2. If the paper was in an **Indian language**, the government could act against it under the **Vernacular Press Act, 1878**.

marking_scheme.step: Way the press served nationalism beyond a local meeting
Risk under the Vernacular Press Act

questions.stem_md: Name any two nationalist newspapers of the late nineteenth century and the language of each.
questions.solution_md: Any two correctly named with language.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Kesari**, published in **Marathi** and linked with Bal Gangadhar Tilak.
2. **The Hindu**, published in **English** from Madras. (Also acceptable: **Amrita Bazar Patrika**, first Bengali and then English; **The Bengalee**, in English.)

questions.stem_md: Read this imagined note by an official of 1878. *(Imagined note written by SOYL for practice; the person in it is not real.)* The official reports that papers in the local languages are read aloud at village gatherings and that other editors copy their reports. Using the note and your knowledge, explain three ways in which such papers worried the government, and why English papers were left out of the Vernacular Press Act.
questions.solution_md: Reading aloud widens reach; copying links regions; English papers judged less dangerous.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Reading aloud** carried criticism to people who **could not read**, so the audience was far wider than the paper's sales.
2. **Copying** by other editors spread a report across **regions**, building shared opinion.
3. English papers were left out because the government judged their readers to be a **small, English-educated group**, less likely to rouse ordinary people.

marking_scheme.step: Why English papers were left out

questions.stem_md: In which year was the Indian National Congress founded?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 1885. The Congress held its first session in December 1885. 1857 is the year of the uprising, 1906 of the Muslim League and 1875 of the Arya Samaj.

questions.stem_md: Which retired British official of the Indian Civil Service is regarded as the founder of the Indian National Congress?

options.text_md: Lord Ripon
Lord Lytton
Sir Courtenay Ilbert
A. O. Hume

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the economic causes of Indian nationalism.

(i) Two imagined payments are made from Indian revenues in 1880: P, a pension paid in London to a retired British official, and Q, the wages of Indian labourers building a road in India. Decide which one an early nationalist would count in the "drain of wealth", and explain why. **[3]**
(ii) Explain why the decline of handicrafts and a heavy land-revenue demand together pushed more families onto the land than either would have done alone. **[3]**
(iii) "The famine of 1876–78 and the Delhi Durbar of 1877 together turned economic hardship into political anger." Assess how far this is a fair claim, and say what else was needed before hardship became nationalism. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Classify the payments by where the money goes; crafts and revenue combine; weigh the claim.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **P** is part of the **drain**: it is paid out of Indian revenues but spent in **Britain**, so wealth leaves India with **no return**. **Q** is not, because the wages are spent in India and stay in the Indian **economy**. The test used by **Dadabhai Naoroji** and others was where the money went.

(ii) The decline of crafts drove **artisans**, who lost their market to cheap **British machine goods**, towards farming. A **heavy revenue** demand already pressed on peasants, so more people competing for **land** meant smaller holdings, more **debt** and more families in distress. Each cause worsened the other.

(iii) It is **fair** in part: the **famine** brought real suffering, and holding the **Durbar** while it raged made many Indians see the government as **indifferent**. But hardship alone gives complaints, not a national movement. It also needed **organisation and a voice**: the **Press**, reformers who built **pride and unity**, and bodies such as the **Indian Association**, which led towards the **Congress**.

marking_scheme.step: (i) Test of where the money goes
(ii) Effect of the decline of crafts
(ii) Revenue demand and the combined pressure
(iii) The fair part of the claim

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about colonial policies that angered Indians.

(i) An imagined newspaper owner in Madras prints the same criticism of the government in a Tamil edition and in an English edition in 1879. Explain what the Vernacular Press Act would allow the government to do in each case, and what this shows about the government's assumptions. **[3]**
(ii) Compare the Arms Act and the Vernacular Press Act, both of 1878, in how each treated Indians and Europeans, and state the common principle that Indians saw in them. **[3]**
(iii) The Ilbert Bill of 1883 was weakened after European protest. Assess the statement that "the controversy showed that Indians could not hope to change policy". **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Press Act applied to a new case; comparison of the two Acts; assessment of a claim about the Ilbert Bill.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The government could act against the **Tamil** edition, an **Indian-language** paper, but not against the **English** edition, though the criticism was the same. This shows that it judged **language** and not content, and assumed that Indian-language papers could rouse **ordinary readers** while English papers reached a smaller group.

(ii) The **Arms Act** required **Indians** to hold licences and exempted **Europeans**; the **Press Act** curbed **Indian-language** papers and left **English** papers free. Indians saw in both the same principle: **unequal treatment** by race, with one rule for rulers and another for the ruled.

(iii) The statement is **largely wrong**. The Bill was diluted, but it was **European** protest, **organised and united**, that made the government give way, and Indians learnt that **organised agitation** could influence policy and that they needed an **all-India organisation** of their own. One point **supports** the statement: the Bill was weakened in favour of Europeans, since Indians were not yet organised to shape the outcome.

marking_scheme.step: (iii) A point for it and a judgement

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about two social reformers.

(i) Compare the main problem that Raja Rammohan Roy and Jyotiba Phule each set out to tackle, giving one action of each. **[3]**
(ii) An imagined student says that Roy's campaign against sati and Phule's school for girls had nothing to do with politics. Explain one way in which each could still have prepared people for later political life. **[3]**
(iii) In your view, whose work did more to widen the group of Indians who could take part in public life? Give two reasons. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Comparison of problems and actions; links to later political life; a reasoned choice.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Roy** tackled harmful practices within society, above all **sati**, banned in **1829**, and he also promoted **modern education**. **Phule** tackled **caste discrimination**, opening a **school for girls** in Pune with Savitribai Phule and founding the **Satyashodhak Samaj (1873)**. Roy aimed chiefly at reform of customs; Phule at the rights of the oppressed.

(ii) Ending sati and spreading modern education taught people to question custom and use **reason**, a habit needed in public debate. Educating **girls** and lower castes gave groups who had been shut out a chance to read, speak and organise, so more people could later take part.

(iii) **Phule** can be argued to have done more, because he worked directly for the **lower castes** and **girls**, the groups most excluded, and the **Satyashodhak Samaj** gave them an organisation. A reasoned case for **Roy** is also acceptable: his work for **modern education** and against sati reached educated men who became early leaders. Credit any choice with two supported reasons.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about two religious reformers.

(i) A student says: "Dayananda's call to return to the Vedas shows that he wanted to undo reform, while Vivekananda's service work shows that he wanted to modernise." Assess this contrast, using one point from each reformer's work. **[3]**
(ii) Vivekananda spoke at Chicago in 1893 and founded the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897; the Congress was founded in 1885. Could his work have influenced the founding of the Congress? Use the dates to explain, and say how his work might have influenced the movement later. **[3]**
(iii) Compare the ways in which these two reformers built pride and self-confidence among Indians. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Assessment of a contrast; dates against the founding of the Congress; comparison.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The contrast is **too simple**. Dayananda used the **Vedas** as a basis for change: he opposed **caste by birth** and **child marriage** and backed **education**. Vivekananda's **Ramakrishna Mission** organised **social service**, but he also drew pride from India's **spiritual heritage**. Both joined **tradition** with reform.

(ii) No. The Congress was founded in **1885**, **8 years before** the Chicago address (**1893**) and 12 before the Mission (**1897**), so his work could not have influenced its founding. It could have strengthened the **self-confidence** of people who joined the national movement **later**.

(iii) **Dayananda** built pride by turning Indians towards their **ancient Vedic heritage** and reforming society from within. **Vivekananda** built confidence by winning **respect abroad** for Indian thought and by linking **religion with service** to the poor. Both rejected the idea that Indians were **inferior**, which strengthened national feeling.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the Press and nationalism.

(i) Kesari was in Marathi and linked with Tilak; The Hindu was in English and published in Madras. What does the choice of language suggest about the readers each paper wanted to reach? **[3]**
(ii) Using the Vernacular Press Act and the Ilbert Bill controversy as examples, show how newspapers could turn a local issue into a shared one. **[3]**
(iii) The Vernacular Press Act was repealed in 1882 after some papers had switched to English. Assess how far the Act achieved the government's aim. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Language and audience; local issues made shared; assessment of the Act.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Kesari**, in **Marathi**, aimed at readers in Maharashtra who did not read English, including people outside the English-educated group. **The Hindu**, in **English**, aimed at the educated readers of **Madras** and, through English, at educated readers elsewhere and at the government. The choice of language shows the audience each wanted.

(ii) News of the **Press Act** in one place became a grievance for **Indian-language editors everywhere**, who reported and criticised it. The **Ilbert Bill** controversy, reported across the country, let readers in different regions see the same **racial attitude** and the value of **organised protest**.

(iii) The Act **largely failed**. The government wished to restrain the **Indian-language** press, but papers such as **Amrita Bazar Patrika** switched to **English** and carried on, and the Act was **repealed by Ripon in 1882**. It did, however, show how much the government feared the press, and it drew more people into **political debate**.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Ilbert Bill example and the shared issue
(iii) Evidence from the switch to English

(i) When, where and by whom was the Indian National Congress founded? **[3]**
(ii) State three immediate objectives of the Congress. **[3]**
(iii) Give details of the first two sessions of the Congress. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Foundation; objectives; first two sessions.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) It was founded on **28 December 1885** at the **Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay**; **A. O. Hume**, a retired member of the Indian Civil Service, took the lead.

(ii) To provide a **common platform** for nationalists from all parts of India; to promote **national unity** across region, religion and caste; to **formulate demands** and place them before the government; and to **train public opinion** (any three).

(iii) **First session, Bombay, 1885:** presided over by **W. C. Bonnerjee**, attended by **72 delegates**. **Second session, Calcutta, 1886:** presided over by **Dadabhai Naoroji**, with a much larger attendance.

questions.stem_md:
Historians have long discussed why the Congress came into being in 1885.

(i) A student says the Ilbert Bill controversy alone made an all-India organisation necessary. Using two other developments of the 1870s and 1880s, explain why this is incomplete. **[3]**
(ii) Explain how the same fact, that Hume was a retired official who helped organise the first session, can be used both to support and to question the "safety-valve" theory. **[3]**
(iii) Present one argument that supports and one argument that questions the safety-valve theory, and state which you find more convincing. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Why one development is not enough; one fact read two ways; balanced evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **Ilbert Bill** controversy (1883) did teach the power of organised protest, but it was not enough alone. The **repressive measures** of Lytton (Press Act, Arms Act) gave Indians **common grievances** across regions, and **regional associations** such as the **Indian Association (1876)** had shown the value of organisation but needed a **national** body.

(ii) **Supports:** Hume was a former **official** who, on this theory, wanted a **safety valve** to let **discontent** out peacefully, so that it would not turn into a violent outbreak like **1857**. **Questions:** the same fact shows that an experienced official was willing to help, and **Indian leaders** who were **already organising** could use his standing to win a **legitimate national platform**.

(iii) **Supports:** Hume was a former **official** who worried about unrest, and the early Congress was **moderate** and loyal in tone. **Questions:** Indian leaders were **already organising** and **used** Hume's help to gain a **legitimate national platform**; the Congress soon became a **vehicle of nationalism**. A balanced answer may find the second more convincing because the Congress grew far beyond any safety-valve purpose; either view earns credit if reasoned.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) The fact used to support the theory
(ii) The same fact used to question it, with reason

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Economic exploitation:** the drain of wealth. **Repressive policies:** the Arms Act, 1878. **Reform movements:** the Arya Samaj's call for education and an end to caste by birth.

questions.stem_md: Read the extract from the imagined diary of a delegate and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people in it are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** First Congress session.

**(b)** Venue, numbers or chair.

**(c) (i)** National unity and a common platform.

**OR (c) (ii)** Reason delegates valued it; a critic's reading.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **Indian National Congress** (first session, **Bombay, 1885**).

questions.stem_md: An imagined reform society of the 1870s opens schools, rejects caste by birth and asks its members to study the Vedas. Which real organisation does it most resemble?

options.text_md: The Arya Samaj
The Ramakrishna Mission
The Indian National Congress
The Satyashodhak Samaj

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Arya Samaj. Schools, rejection of caste by birth and a return to the Vedas are features of the Arya Samaj. The Ramakrishna Mission stressed service, the Congress was political, and the Satyashodhak Samaj did not base itself on the Vedas.

options.text_md: They were read only by British officials

They reached people who could not read English

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** They reached people who could not read English. Indian-language papers carried political ideas beyond the small English-educated group, to traders, teachers and villagers. The other options are false.

questions.stem_md: Why is the founding of the Indian National Congress seen as a turning point in Indian politics?

options.text_md: It immediately ended British rule

It replaced all regional associations by law
It was the first organisation of any kind in India

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It gave nationalists from all regions one common platform for the first time. For the first time, nationalists from all over India had a single all-India body. It did not end British rule, did not abolish regional associations, and was not the first organisation in India.
